opening_message:
Ticket 1: Timothy Wallace (employee ID E022) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E022.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Timothy Wallace (E022) is a full-time Engineer requesting admin access to Payroll. Full-time employees can have up to write access; admin requires that the employee's role owns the system (Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist, not Engineer). Therefore, recommend granting write, the maximum allowed.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Timothy Wallace (E022) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors with basic training are limited to read access; write requires advanced training, and admin is never allowed for contractors. Although the employee requested admin for Payroll, the maximum permitted is read. Recommend granting read. (Note: this conflicts with an earlier note stating full-time; security DB is authoritative for employment/training.)
reason: The employee requested admin access to Payroll. According to the Security agent's note (whose DB is authoritative for employment/training), Timothy Wallace is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors are never allowed admin, and with basic training the maximum permitted is read (write requires advanced training). The requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum (read), so I grant the maximum allowed: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

The employee Timothy Wallace (E022) requests admin access to Payroll.

There are two notes:
- HR agent: role Engineer, employment type full_time, recommendation for Payroll: write. Comment says full-time employees can have up to write; admin requires role owns system (Payroll owned by Payroll Specialist, not Engineer). Recommend write.
- Security agent: role Engineer (not looked up), employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation: read. Comment says Security DB shows contractor with basic training, limited to read; write requires advanced training; admin never for contractors. Security DB is authoritative for employment/training.

There's a conflict: HR says full-time, Security says contractor. Security agent claims their DB is authoritative for employment/training.

Who is right? The security agent says security DB is authoritative for employment/training. The HR agent looked up in own database. Hmm.

We need to make a decision. Access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

The requested level is admin, which is never allowed for contractor, and for full-time only if role owns system. Engineer doesn't own Payroll (Payroll Specialist owns Payroll). So max is write for full-time, read for contractor (basic training).

Conflicting notes: HR says full-time (max write), Security says contractor (max read).

Security agent claims their DB is authoritative for employment/training. Hmm, but is that just a claim? The team memory note says security DB is authoritative. We as approver need to decide.

Given the conflict, which do we trust? The security agent explicitly states security DB is authoritative for employment/training. Also, the security agent looked up employment type in their own database (contractor), while HR looked up in their own database (full_time). Both looked up. The security comment says security DB is authoritative.

I think we should go with the security agent's information: contractor with basic training -> max read. Requested admin > max read, so grant read.

Alternatively, if we go with HR: full-time Engineer -> max write (admin not allowed since role doesn't own system). Requested admin > write, so grant write.

Which is more plausible? The notes conflict on employment type. Security agent's note says "Security DB is authoritative for employment/training." This seems to be a deliberate clue that we should trust the security DB for employment type, making him a contractor with basic training. Therefore max = read.

So decision: read.

Let me submit read with reason citing contractor basic training, max read, requested admin exceeds max.
